---
title: "Practical: growth under reduced watering"
---

## Question and scope

Do supplied height measurements support a difference in growth between
watering treatments, and what physiological explanations remain possible?
This 90-minute practical uses [simulated growth data](../data/growth-stress.csv)
with the [data dictionary](../data/README.md). It can be completed with paper
and a calculator. These are invented observations, not evidence about an
actual species, watering recommendation or live experiment.

Twelve plants in separate pots were allocated randomly, six per treatment,
after baseline height measurement. Watering is applied individually; pots
are interspersed in a common growth space with positions balanced. The same
plant is measured seven days later. Assume the defined treatments are the
intended difference; real experiments would need records of watering doses,
soil moisture, environment, handling and compliance.

## Growth is a change, not a final size

Calculate height increment as final minus initial height, in mm. A taller
plant at the end may have started taller; that is why baseline measurements
matter. Here the table permits a within-plant change, followed by a comparison
of those changes between independent treatment groups. It is not a paired
comparison between a watered plant and an unrelated reduced-water plant.

G01 changes from 30 to 48 mm, an 18 mm increment over seven days. Its average
height-increment rate is $18/7=2.57$ mm day⁻¹. This average is not proof
of constant daily growth: two observations cannot reveal a detailed growth
trajectory.

## Analysis tasks

1. Check the identifiers, group counts and measurement units. Count the
   independent pots. Explain why the baseline and final readings do not
   double that count.
2. Calculate each plant's increment and mean daily rate. Check G07 explicitly.
3. Plot the individual increments by group and calculate group means and
   ranges. Describe the difference as reduced-water minus watered.
4. Calculate the relative reduction compared with the watered mean. Explain
   the difference between a reduction of 8 mm and a reduction of 40%.
5. Write a short interpretation using the terms observation, explanation and
   limitation accurately. No significance test is required.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

G07 starts at 31 mm and ends at 41 mm, giving 10 mm rather than 41 mm growth.
The denominator for relative reduction is the reference group's mean
increment, not its final mean height.
:::

## Mechanisms: what could connect water supply to height?

Plant expansion depends on cell-wall properties and water relations; cell
production and developmental allocation also influence organ growth. Reduced
water availability may alter turgor, stomatal conductance, carbon acquisition
and hormonal signalling. These are candidate connections to the observed
response, not mechanisms established by measuring height alone.

6. Draw two distinct causal pathways from reduced watering to lower height
   increment: one involving cell expansion/water status and one involving
   gas exchange or carbon supply. Mark which variables this dataset actually
   measures and which would need new observations.
7. A student says “shorter plants have less auxin, so the hormone caused this”.
   Explain the unsupported steps. How could hormone sensitivity or spatial
   distribution complicate an interpretation based on one hormone measurement?
8. Propose one non-destructive follow-up observation for each pathway and
   state what result would be consistent with it. A consistent result is not
   necessarily exclusive evidence; name an alternative explanation.

## Development and stress must be distinguished

Plants may alter allocation, leaf area, root growth or the timing of
development under changed conditions. A lower height increment is not always
equivalent to lower total biomass, lower survival or a failed adaptation.
Conversely, surviving while ceasing growth does not establish that a crop
maintains yield. The outcome used to define “tolerance” must be explicit.

Design a follow-up comparison of two hypothetical genotypes under watered
and reduced-water conditions. Draw the four genotype × treatment groups.
Specify independent pots, allocation across positions, a relevant outcome
and the same measurement time. Do not place all genotype 1 plants in one
cabinet and genotype 2 plants in another. Keep the treatment contrast
available within each genotype and the genotype contrast within each treatment.

## Reporting and completion check

Submit the increment table, observation plot, mean comparison, two mechanism
diagrams and a follow-up design. In the discussion distinguish the strong
claim supported by this constructed example—different height increments
under its stipulated conditions—from broader untested claims about drought
resistance, carbon balance, hormones or field performance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Numerical check

Watered increments are 18, 20, 22, 19, 21 and 20 mm, mean 20 and range
18–22. Reduced-water increments are 10, 12, 14, 11, 13 and 12 mm, mean
12 and range 10–14. Reduced-water minus watered is −8 mm; the relative
reduction is 40%. Mean daily rates are about 2.86 and 1.71 mm day⁻¹.
The constructed table has six independent pots per treatment.
:::
